defaults.permitted_development: Across West Sussex, demolition is controlled by the GPDO and heritage legislation rather than treated as a free-standing general right. The route depends on what is being removed, whether Part 11 applies and whether the building or site is protected.

rules.height_rules: There is no demolition height allowance. Height matters because it affects method, sequencing, temporary works, visibility and the risk posed to adjoining land and buildings.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth rule. Partial demolition and demolition tied to rebuilding have to be judged by the real scope of the works and by what remains on site afterwards.
rules.boundary_rules: Across West Sussex, the practical boundary issues are usually neighbour safety, party structures, plant access, hoarding, highway occupation and the stability of anything left standing next door.
rules.roof_rules: Roof removal is not automatically a clean separate step. Once it forms part of wider demolition, heritage, structural stability and weatherproofing can alter the planning route.
rules.materials_rules: Salvage, asbestos, dust, waste removal and making good exposed faces are usually the live practical issues. Separate health, safety and building-control duties remain in play even where the planning route is clear.

rules.permitted_development: Demolition is controlled through the GPDO and heritage law, not treated as an uncomplicated general right. In Adur, demolition on prominent sites is usually judged as much by how the works are managed as by what is being taken down.

rules.height_rules: For demolition, height is a practical issue rather than a permitted envelope: taller structures usually mean more complex sequencing and greater neighbour impact. rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth rule. Partial demolition, demolition tied to rebuilding, or removal of only part of a structure must be judged on the actual scope of works and any linked development.
rules.boundary_rules: The harder boundary questions are often about hoarding, access routes, adjoining structures and what protection nearby occupiers will actually get during the works. rules.roof_rules: Taking off a roof is not automatically a standalone permitted step. Where roof removal forms part of wider demolition, heritage, structural and weatherproofing issues can change the planning route.
rules.materials_rules: Salvage, recycling, asbestos handling, waste removal and making good exposed surfaces are key practical issues. Separate environmental and building-control duties still apply even where the planning route is clear. On coastal sites, exposure, public safety and how the cleared site will be secured and finished are often especially important.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status can move demolition onto a much tighter footing, especially where the building or enclosure contributes to the setting.
restrictions.listed_building: If the structure is listed, or protected by curtilage listing, demolition sits on a listed building consent footing rather than an ordinary demolition route.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction can still disapply the simpler demolition route for the exact site.
